from pypdf import PdfReader
from pathlib import Path
r=PdfReader('manuscript.pdf')
p=Path('tmp/pdfs'); p.mkdir(parents=True,exist_ok=True)
print('PAGES',len(r.pages))
print('METADATA',r.metadata)
parts=[]
for i,page in enumerate(r.pages):
    t=page.extract_text()
    parts.append('\\n========== PAGE '+str(i+1)+' ==========\\n'+t)
(p/'manuscript.txt').write_text('\\n'.join(parts))
print('\\n'.join(parts[:3]))
PY"

strengths: Addresses an important microscopy problem: recovering explicit 3D cell surfaces without annotated training datasets. Mesh outputs are useful for geometric measurements and biophysical modeling.

The integration of continuous surface densities, Fourier-domain image formation, and differentiable PSF optimization is coherent. Custom CUDA kernels and frequency truncation address a substantial computational bottleneck.

Experiments include varied synthetic shapes and real organoid and embryo images. On 15 organoid volumes, reported image-reconstruction results improve over DM3D: MSE decreases from 0.0125 to 0.0020, and SSIM increases from 0.7101 to 0.8021.
The manuscript acknowledges related PSF-aware active contours and credits the principal datasets, geometry-processing methods, and optimization techniques it uses.
weaknesses: The central claim of accurate cell geometry lacks independent quantitative validation. Sections 6.2–6.3 evaluate rendered-image similarity rather than surface accuracy or instance segmentation. Rendering both methods with deltaMic’s inferred PSF can favor its fitted solution; improved photometric agreement does not establish improved geometry. Surface-distance or overlap measurements are particularly feasible for the synthetic examples, where reference meshes exist.

Joint shape–PSF recovery is insufficiently demonstrated. Synthetic experiments use the same Gaussian PSF for generation and inference, while real examples provide no independently measured PSF or quantitative PSF error. Consequently, the evidence does not establish whether the recovered optical parameters are meaningful or compensate for shape/model errors. A fixed-versus-learned PSF ablation and controlled joint-recovery experiments are needed.

Several mathematical statements require correction. Under the stated Fourier convention, the Gaussian transform contains Σ rather than Σ inverse. The sparse system in Section 5.2 is not equivalent to the preceding smoothing update, and Eqs. (11)–(12) use inconsistent exponential signs. These could be transcription errors rather than implementation failures, but corrected formulas and numerical gradient validation are necessary for a reproducible technical specification.

The claim of eliminating heuristic priors is overstated. Although there is no explicit shape penalty, optimization uses Laplacian gradient smoothing with λ = 50, topology-informed initialization, and known cell counts for embryos. Ablations do not separate the effects of the physical renderer, gradient smoothing, weighted loss, and mesh resolution. This leaves the source of smoothness and robustness unclear.

Originality needs sharper positioning against the acknowledged PSF-aware contour methods [25,57] and Euclidean spectral transformation work [30]. The manuscript does not clearly establish which Fourier-transform components are new versus adaptations, or experimentally isolate the benefit of its formulation over these closely related approaches.

Practical reproducibility and efficiency remain insufficiently documented. Learning rates, intensity normalization, covariance constraints, and the alternation schedule are unspecified, and no code availability statement is provided. Forward-rendering benchmarks do not establish end-to-end runtime or memory for the 10,000-step reconstructions. Several figure captions also describe different content from their associated figures, making the experimental evidence unnecessarily difficult to follow.
